opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a model that makes sense in a very specific moment, but I have real doubts about whether it can carry the industry forward on its own.

The logic is easy to see. Everyone agrees that data is the bottleneck for embodied intelligence. We don't have an internet-scale corpus for robot actions the way language models had text. So some companies say: let's sell hardware to universities, labs, and data-collection factories, people teleoperate the robots, and that data flows back to build a foundation model. It also produces revenue early, which matters when investors keep asking when you'll make money.

But think about the economics. Teleoperation data is extremely expensive. You need the robot, which isn't cheap. You need a trained operator. And in a full working day one person gets maybe a few hundred, maybe a thousand, valid trajectories for one kind of task. Compare that with the scale behind GPT-style models. If the amount of data you need is several orders of magnitude beyond what teleoperation produces, you can't close that gap by hiring more people. The cost curve doesn't come down fast enough.

There's also a quality and diversity problem. Teleoperated data tends to cluster: the same tables, the same objects, the same lighting, a few operators' habits. It's good for fitting a task, but generalization comes from diversity, and teleoperation is weakest exactly there. And once the hardware changes, a new hand or new arm kinematics, a lot of that data loses value.

As a business, selling machines for data collection is really selling shovels during a gold rush. It works while everyone's digging, but the buyers are mostly research institutions and other robotics companies, not end users who need robots to do real work. That market is finite. If the robot can't do useful work afterward, the demand eventually dries up.

My own view, and it's what we've been betting on at Galbot, is that the base of the data pyramid has to be synthetic: large-scale simulation and generated data, where you control diversity and the marginal cost is close to zero. We've shown that grasping and some navigation and manipulation skills can be trained almost entirely in simulation and transferred zero-shot to the real world. Real data is still important, but as the tip of the pyramid, for alignment and fine-tuning and closing the sim-to-real gap, not as the main fuel.

The best real data comes from robots deployed doing actual jobs, in pharmacies, factories, retail, where every hour of operation produces value and data together. That flywheel is sustainable. Paying people to teleoperate robots just to make data is more like a transitional phase. It's not wrong, but I don't think it's where the endgame is.

fable-5.1.text:
I think this model has a logic to it, but I'm honestly skeptical about whether it's a sustainable path to embodied intelligence.

Let's start with what's attractive about it. Real-world data is the biggest bottleneck in robotics right now. We don't have an internet-scale dataset of robot actions the way language models had text. So if you can sell hardware, get it into customers' hands, and have them teleoperate the robots to generate data, you're turning a cost center into a revenue stream. Customers pay you for the machine, and you also get the data flywheel. On paper that's very elegant.

But there are a few problems I keep coming back to.

First, the quality and distribution of teleoperation data. When a human is driving the robot through a controller or a VR setup, the motions you get reflect human reaction time, the latency of the system, and the limitations of the interface. The data is biased toward whatever tasks are easy to teleoperate, not necessarily what we need the robot to learn. And it's expensive per sample. You're paying a human to be a slow, imperfect robot.

Second, there's an incentive mismatch. The customer bought the robot to get work done. If the robot can't do useful work autonomously yet, the customer is essentially paying you to do data labeling for you. That's a hard sell at scale. Early adopters and research labs will do it, but ordinary industrial customers want ROI, not a research partnership. So the volume you actually get is limited.

Third, I think there's a deeper question about whether teleoperation data is even the right foundation. My view has been that we should lean heavily on simulation and synthetic data for the bulk of learning, especially for things like grasping and manipulation where physics can be modeled reasonably well, and then use a smaller amount of real data to close the sim-to-real gap. If you build your entire company around collecting real demonstrations one at a time, you're competing on a resource that doesn't scale the way compute does.

So my assessment is that it's a reasonable bridge strategy. It helps a company survive, build relationships with customers, and gather some real-world signal. But I wouldn't mistake it for the destination. The companies that win will be the ones that figure out how to generate most of their training signal cheaply, through simulation, video, or large-scale internet data, and use real-world data as a correction rather than the main course.

astra-6.text:
I think it can work as an early-stage business model, but we should separate two things: selling a robot that creates value for the customer, and using that robot to collect data that improves the system.

If the customer has a real task to perform, and teleoperation lets them perform it reliably at an acceptable cost, then there’s a reasonable starting point. You can collect data from actual work and gradually automate more of it. But if the main proposition is, “Buy our machine and operate it so we can get training data,” the incentives are harder to align. The customer is paying for the hardware and providing the labor, while much of the potential future benefit goes to the robot company.

The other question is whether the data is actually useful. Hours of teleoperation don’t automatically translate into better autonomy. You need relevant tasks, consistent data quality, and a way to test whether training on that data improves performance in deployment.

So I would judge this model by the transition it enables: does the amount of human intervention fall while the robot continues to deliver value? If that happens, teleoperation can be a bridge to a sustainable business. If it doesn’t, you have to make the economics work as a remotely operated service.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it can be a reasonable starting point, but selling machines and building a data flywheel are two different things. Customers buy a robot because it does useful work, not because they want to collect training data for you. If they still need someone operating it all the time, you have to ask whether the economics actually work once you include that labor.

The other question is whether the data you collect helps you reduce that dependence on teleoperation. More hours of data don’t automatically translate into better autonomy. The tasks need to be relevant, the data needs to be usable, and you need a way to measure whether each round of training improves performance.

So I’d judge this model by the transition it enables. Can the robot deliver value initially with human assistance, then require less assistance over time? If that loop works, selling machines can help you scale both deployment and learning. If it doesn’t, you may simply be scaling a remotely operated service.
